Shoulder Pain

tendon vs joint by range of motion · cuff, impingement and biceps · red flags and referred pain · never a slingIs passive motion preserved, and what has the patient already tried?

1Presentation2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Presentation
Bottom line
  • Sort by range of motion: active lost with passive kept is a tendon; both lost is the joint; a normal shoulder exam means referred pain
  • Cuff tendinopathy is clinical (painful arc, Neer, Hawkins): rest and an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug), then cuff strengthening, then occasionally an injection for short-term relief; MRI for weakness or failed therapy
  • Rest never means a sling for tendon pain: prolonged immobilization is a risk factor for adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)
What it is

Shoulder pain in an adult, from a tendon, the joint, or somewhere else

Sort by

Active against passive range of motion, then the maneuvers

Hands off

A hot, swollen shoulder: Hot Joint or Bursa in an Adult; glenohumeral osteoarthritis (degenerative joint disease): Osteoarthritis

2Urgent risks
Septic arthritisFever, a red swollen shoulder that refuses all motion

If the joint is hot and swollen, choose arthrocentesis before antibiotics.

Referred cardiac painExertional pain with a normal shoulder exam

If the shoulder exam is normal and the pain is exertional, choose an electrocardiogram (ECG).

Pancoast tumorA stiff, painful shoulder with cough or dyspnea
3Differential
Shoulder pain, most tempting first
DiagnosisFingerprintDecides it
Rotator cuff tendinopathy or impingementOverhead use; pain worst between 60 and 120 degrees of abductionPassive motion kept; Neer, Hawkins or empty can positive Cuff maneuversEmpty can (Jobe): resisted downward pressure on the arms forward-flexed with thumbs down tests the supraspinatus. Neer: a positive test is impingement of the cuff tendons under the coracoacromial arch. Weak resisted external rotation suggests significant cuff dysfunction, such as a complete tear.
Full-thickness rotator cuff tearWeakness more than pain, in abduction and external rotationAcute, after a fall or injury: MRI confirms
Biceps tendinopathy (biceps tendinitis)Anterior shoulder painTender long head of the biceps; Speed or Yergason test positive
Adhesive capsulitis (frozen shoulder)Woman aged 40 to 60; diabetes, thyroid disease or dyslipidemia; or after immobilizationChronic, over months; active and passive motion lost in two or more planes, external rotation and abduction most
Calcific tendinopathySevere pain on abductionPassive motion kept; calcium in the tendon on the radiograph
Glenohumeral osteoarthritisOlder; prior shoulder trauma or surgeryMotion lost like adhesive capsulitis; radiograph
Acromioclavicular joint injuryTrauma to the top of the shoulderPain on cross-arm adduction; glenohumeral motion kept
C5 to C6 radiculopathyNeck pain on movement, hand weakness or numbnessNormal shoulder exam; neck signs
4Workup
Tendon pain: start on the lowest rung not yet tried
RungDoMove on when
1Stop the offending activity; an NSAID; no slingNo better after a brief trial
2Physical therapy to strengthen the cuffPain persists
3Subacromial glucocorticoid injection Steroid injectionA subacromial glucocorticoid injection gives short-term relief; repeated injections risk tendon degeneration, so limit them.Still failing, or a tear suspected
4MRI, then surgeryTop rung

Adhesive capsulitis takes a different plan: Adhesive capsulitis treatmentAn NSAID and gentle physical therapy (aggressive stretching makes it worse); an intra-articular glucocorticoid injection early, alongside therapy; oral glucocorticoids help only briefly; surgical release when refractory.

Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Weeks in a sling after a minor injury, now stiff in every directionAdhesive capsulitis from immobilizationPhysical therapy, not more rest
Young patient, traumatic full-thickness tearA repairable tearPrompt orthopedic referral for repair
Bulge in the arm after a sudden load on the flexed elbowBiceps tendon rupture, proximal (long head) or distalProximal: reassurance and follow-up; distal: surgical repair, especially if young or active
Scapular winging after axillary node dissection, or supraspinatus and infraspinatus atrophyLong thoracic nerve (serratus anterior) or suprascapular nerve (C5 to C6)Recognize the nerve; no cuff workup
Fall on the shoulder, midshaft tendernessClavicle fractureUsually conservative; a sling is right here
Force on an arm held out and turned out; it stays that way, deltoid flattenedAnterior dislocation, by far the most common; labrum (Bankart) and humeral head (Hill-Sachs) injuriesRadiographs, prompt closed reduction; test lateral shoulder sensation (axillary nerve)
Seizure or electrocution; arm held in and turned in, cannot turn outPosterior dislocation, easy to miss on filmsAxillary view
Dislocation with a humeral neck fractureFracture-dislocation: no closed reductionEmergency orthopedic consultation for surgical reduction
A dislocation, reducedRecurrence if under 25 in contact sports; a cuff tear if over 40Sling for 1 to 3 weeks, then physical therapy

Pause point. The bait: a sling or "just rest" for tendon pain, or MRI first. Start on the lowest rung not yet tried, and keep the shoulder moving.

Practice
  1. 58-year-old man has 2 months of right shoulder pain pain arcs between 60 and 120 degrees of abduction active abduction limited; passive abduction full Paints ceilings for work Afebrile · empty can test painful · Neer test positive → Rotator cuff tendinopathy → active motion lost with passive motion kept is a tendon problem: rotator cuff tendinopathy; relative rest and physical therapy
  2. 62-year-old woman with diabetes has 4 months of shoulder stiffness both active and passive motion lost in every plane external rotation most limited Wore a sling for a wrist fracture Afebrile · no crepitus · strength normal within the motion she has → Adhesive capsulitis → active and passive motion both lost points to the joint; diabetes and immobilization favor adhesive capsulitis
  3. 70-year-old man cannot lift his right arm overhead cannot initiate abduction drop-arm test positive: the arm falls from 90 degrees Weakness worse than pain since a fall Afebrile · passive motion full · no neck pain → Full-thickness rotator cuff tear → a positive drop-arm test is a full-thickness rotator cuff tear: MRI, which is ordered here and not for tendinopathy
  4. 55-year-old man with diabetes has a hot, swollen right shoulder refuses all movement, active or passive visible effusion Pain began 2 days ago Fever, T 38.9 °C · HR 108/min · white cells 16,000/mm³ → Septic arthritis → fever, effusion and refusal of all movement is septic arthritis: aspirate before antibiotics, and never inject steroid into it
  5. 48-year-old man has right shoulder pain radiating below the elbow numbness of the thumb neck extension and rotation reproduce the pain Shoulder range of motion full and painless Afebrile · biceps reflex reduced on the right → C5–C6 radiculopathy → pain past the elbow with thumb numbness and a normal shoulder exam is a C5 to C6 radiculopathy; Spurling is positive
  6. 60-year-old man has left shoulder pain when he climbs stairs pain on exertion, relieved within minutes by rest diaphoresis with the episodes Smoker with hypertension BP 152/90 mm Hg · HR 84/min · shoulder examination normal → Referred cardiac pain → exertional shoulder pain with a normal shoulder exam is referred cardiac pain: ECG (electrocardiogram)
  7. 58-year-old man treated for a painful arc returns at 3 weeks has kept his arm in the sling ever since passive motion now starting to stiffen Was given a sling at the first visit Afebrile · painful arc persists → Continued sling immobilization → continued sling immobilization is how adhesive capsulitis follows a cuff problem; slings are for dislocation and fracture
  8. 26-year-old man has 3 weeks of anterior right shoulder pain tender over the bicipital groove still throwing weekly: pitches in a league every weekend No treatment yet Afebrile · pain on resisted supination with the elbow flexed → Activity modification plus NSAIDs → the least-intensive step comes first: activity modification and an NSAID (nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug); injection and surgery come much later
  9. 26-year-old man, a pitcher, has persistent anterior shoulder pain still painful after 6 weeks of activity modification and NSAIDs tender over the bicipital groove No weakness, locking or night pain Afebrile · range of motion full · strength normal → Physical therapy → not improving after a brief trial of activity change and an NSAID: physical therapy is the next rung, before injection or MRI
  10. 62-year-old man felt a pop in his right arm while lifting a box bulge in the mid upper arm when he flexes mild ache, little weakness Elbow crease not tender Afebrile · supination strength nearly normal → Long head of biceps rupture → a proximal (long head) rupture leaves a bulge in the mid arm and is treated without surgery in older adults
  11. 26-year-old man has anterior right shoulder pain after weekend throwing pain reproduced by resisted supination with the elbow flexed tender over the bicipital groove No clicking or locking Afebrile · painful arc absent → Biceps tendinitis → groove tenderness with pain on resisted supination and elbow flexion is biceps tendinitis
  12. 45-year-old man has anterior shoulder pain with overhead work strength normal on resisted abduction painful arc of abduction No groove tenderness Afebrile · a positive Hawkins test · passive range of motion full → Subacromial impingement → a positive Hawkins test with a painful arc is subacromial impingement, part of the cuff tendinopathy spectrum
  13. 45-year-old man has sudden antecubital pain after lifting a heavy cabinet weak supination of the forearm gap palpable above the elbow crease Bruising spreads into the forearm the next day Afebrile · biceps hook test abnormal → Urgent orthopedic referral for surgical repair → a distal biceps rupture is repaired surgically, unlike a proximal one: urgent orthopedic referral
Transferable rule

Range of motion sorts tendon from joint before any test. The next step is usually the next rung not yet tried, and every instruction to rest says what to do instead.
